title: Conquest of Bashan
overview: Deuteronomy chapter 3 recounts the victorious conquest of King Og of Bashan and his territory by the Israelites under Moses' leadership. This chapter highlights God's faithfulness in delivering formidable enemies into Israel's hands, the distribution of the conquered lands to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, and Moses' poignant request to enter the Promised Land, which God denies. The chapter serves as a powerful reminder of God's sovereign power, the fulfillment of His promises, and the importance of obedience and trust in His plans. It also sets the stage for Joshua's leadership and Israel's future inheritance, emphasizing God's ongoing guidance and provision.
structure:
**Verses 1-7: The Battle with Og King of Bashan.** The chapter opens with the confrontation and defeat of Og, a giant king, demonstrating God's deliverance and Israel's complete victory.

**Verses 8-11: Description of the Conquered Territory.** This section details the extent of the land taken from the Amorite kings, including notable geographic landmarks and the impressive size of Og’s iron bed.

**Verses 12-17: Allocation of the Land.** Moses describes the division of the conquered land among the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, outlining specific boundaries.

**Verses 18-22: Instructions for the Tribes and Encouragement to Joshua.** Moses commands the tribes to remain armed and protect their inheritance while encouraging Joshua with assurance of God’s continued help.

**Verses 23-29: Moses’ Prayer and God’s Denial.** Moses pleads to enter the Promised Land but is denied by God; instead, he is shown the land from Mount Pisgah and instructed to encourage Joshua.

**Verse 30: The Israelites’ Encampment.** The chapter concludes with the Israelites settling in the valley opposite Bethpeor, preparing for the next phase of their journey.

keyVerses.text: And the LORD said unto me, Fear him not: for I will deliver him, and all his people, and his land, into thy hand; and thou shalt do unto him as thou didst unto Sihon king of the Amorites, which dwelt at Heshbon.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals God's direct encouragement and promise of victory, emphasizing His sovereignty and faithfulness to Israel. It connects to the theme of trusting God's power over seemingly insurmountable enemies.

keyVerses.text: For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of giants; behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron; is it not in Rabbath of the children of Ammon? nine cubits was the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it, after the cubit of a man.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the extraordinary size and strength of Og, underscoring the miraculous nature of Israel’s victory. It also connects to the biblical motif of giants and God’s power over all creation.

keyVerses.text: Ye shall not fear them: for the LORD your God he shall fight for you.
keyVerses.significance: This verse encapsulates the chapter’s central message of divine protection and encouragement, assuring Israel that God fights on their behalf and they need not fear their enemies.

keyVerses.text: But the LORD was wroth with me for your sakes, and would not hear me: and the LORD said unto me, Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto me of this matter.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals the human limitation of Moses despite his faithfulness, showing God’s sovereign will and the necessity of obedience even in disappointment.

characters.name: Moses
characters.description: The leader of Israel who commands the conquest, allocates the land, and intercedes with God to enter the Promised Land. His role is pivotal as mediator, commander, and prophet.

characters.name: Og, King of Bashan
characters.description: The last of the Rephaim giants, a formidable enemy defeated by Israel. His defeat symbolizes God's power over giants and enemies of His people.

characters.name: God (The LORD)
characters.description: The sovereign deliverer who commands, promises victory, and directs the distribution of land. God also denies Moses’ request to enter the Promised Land, demonstrating His ultimate authority.

characters.name: Joshua
characters.description: The appointed successor to Moses, encouraged and strengthened by Moses to lead Israel into the Promised Land and inherit the territories God has given.

themes.description: God’s intervention in battle is central, as He promises and accomplishes the defeat of Og and his people, reinforcing His role as protector and provider for Israel.
Israel’s obedience in conquering and dividing the land reflects trust in God’s promises, while Moses’ submission to God’s will highlights faithful obedience despite personal desires.
The chapter emphasizes God’s control over history and human affairs, from granting victory to denying Moses’ request, underscoring that God’s plans prevail.
The preparation for Joshua’s leadership marks a significant transition, with Moses encouraging him to be strong and courageous, pointing to God’s ongoing guidance.

historicalContext: Deuteronomy 3 is set during the Israelites’ wilderness wanderings, shortly before their entrance into Canaan in the late Bronze Age (circa 1400s BC). The land of Bashan, east of the Jordan River, was a fertile and strategically important region ruled by Amorite kings like Og. The Amorites were a dominant Canaanite people known for their fortified cities and military strength. The conquest reflects the ancient Near Eastern practice of total warfare and land allotment to tribes as part of covenant fulfillment. The mention of giants (Rephaim) connects to ancient traditions of mighty warriors, emphasizing the miraculous nature of Israel’s victories under God’s guidance.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This perspective sees the conquest as a demonstration of God’s sovereign justice and faithfulness to His covenant promises. The denial of Moses’ request highlights God’s righteous judgment and the importance of divine timing.

Dispensationalists emphasize the literal fulfillment of God’s promises to Israel, viewing the conquest and land allocation as a key step in God’s prophetic plan for the nation, with Joshua’s leadership marking a new dispensation.

Early church interpreters often saw Og’s defeat as symbolic of Christ’s victory over sin and death, with Moses’ intercession prefiguring Christ’s mediatory role and the promise of a heavenly inheritance.

application: Trust God’s promises even when facing overwhelming challenges, knowing He fights for His people.
Obey God’s commands faithfully, even when personal desires conflict with His will, as Moses exemplifies.
Encourage and strengthen others in leadership roles, following Moses’ example with Joshua.
Recognize God’s sovereignty over all circumstances and submit to His timing and plans.
Remember that victories and blessings come from God alone, fostering humility and gratitude.
Prepare diligently for responsibilities God entrusts to you, relying on His strength and guidance.
conclusion: Deuteronomy 3 stands as a testament to God’s mighty power, faithfulness, and sovereign will in the history of Israel. Through the conquest of Og and the allocation of the land, believers see the fulfillment of divine promises and the importance of obedience and trust. Moses’ leadership and his submission to God’s plan, alongside the commissioning of Joshua, remind Christians today of the need for faithful stewardship, courage, and reliance on God’s strength. This chapter encourages believers to face their own battles with confidence that God fights for them and to embrace His timing and purposes with humble obedience.
